Good, I have current postings. Here's the comparison — but I'll frame it around what it tells you about the interview, since that's our job here.

The pattern across both companies: they don't really hire generic PMs. Almost every role is wrapped around a specific surface — OpenAI has roles for Integrity, Families, Countries & Governments; Anthropic has Agent Platform/MCP, Claude Code, Claude Growth, Research. So the first thing the requirements tell you is that the interview will be domain-loaded. You're not interviewing for "AIPM," you're interviewing for "PM of agent eval systems" or "PM of growth," and the screen tests that domain.

Where they differ:

OpenAI's postings lean heavily on safety, policy, and deployment language — "safely deploy them to the world," collaboration with safety/policy/user-ops teams. That signals their PM interviews probe how you reason about risk and rollout under scrutiny, not just shipping features. Expect judgment questions about tradeoffs when a capability is powerful but risky.

Anthropic is more explicit about a technical/engineering bar. The Claude Code role literally asks for "5+ years in product management and engineering, including at least 1 year as a professional engineer." For you coming from SWE that's an advantage — they're signaling they want PMs who can sit at the research/eng intersection and not get lost. Their postings repeatedly mention "translating research capabilities into product" and "working with Research teams to define capability and safety assessments."

The common thread that matters most for interview prep: both want product sense + technical depth + hands-on AI experience together (that Aakash Gupta playbook result names exactly those three). Most candidates have one or two.

Two of those three are owned by sibling nodes — the technical depth and hands-on AI work (eval, prompt engineering, agent systems) live in "Skills to build up," and proving the hands-on experience lives in "Portfolio." So I'd send you there for building those.

What's left for *this* node is the third leg: how the interview actually tests product sense and judgment for an AI product. Want me to go into what that loop typically looks like — the product-sense round, the AI-specific case, the behavioral?
